opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Irina, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course, happy to help. I spend all day talking to strangers, so this is easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is useful for us. It translates for guests and writes the review replies. The desk still needs a smile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mobile check-in has already made the desk smaller, so that's not new. In this picture I keep going with my plan to move into revenue management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the online course in hotel revenue management, ask my manager to let me shadow the revenue team one day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I feel in control.

S0.say: AI translates for guests and writes review replies. The desk still needs a smile.
S0.think: The desk is already shrinking, but she can keep to her plan of moving into revenue management.
S0.do: Finishes an online revenue management course and asks to shadow the revenue team weekly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hotels will always need people who make guests feel welcome. But the desk will be smaller, for sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they hire fewer beginners, my front desk team shrinks. I'd be supervising three people instead of six, or the role merges with something. That's why I want to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Push harder for the revenue job. Learn the pricing software they use. Maybe look at other hotel groups if mine doesn't have a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. But I have a plan.

S1.say: Hotels will always need people who make guests feel welcome, but the desk will be smaller.
S1.think: Her team would shrink or her role merge, which is why she wants to move.
S1.do: Pushes for the revenue job, learns the pricing software, and looks at other hotel groups.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, but has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hospitality is about people, and it's still a good place to work. I'd tell my team not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd tell your team not to panic. Would you be panicking a little yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, a little. But I'm the supervisor. If I look scared, they're scared. I'm good at keeping calm on the outside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But the job I wanted is exactly the routine office work this is talking about. Pricing rooms is numbers and rules. An AI agent could do it. So my plan has a hole in it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay at the desk for now, since it's safer than I thought. Learn the guest experience side, events, maybe group sales, where you still meet clients. And save, because we have almost nothing put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. The ladder I was climbing is moving.

S2.say: Hospitality is about people and still a good place to work. Don't panic.
S2.think: Her planned move into revenue management is exactly the routine office work AI agents would take.
S2.do: Stays at the desk for now, learns events and group sales, and starts saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a hard time, but rich travellers will still want good hotels. Maybe even more now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If shares boom, luxury travel booms. That could help me if I move to a nicer hotel. But my husband and I rent, and rent would go up with house prices. We'd have no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply to five-star hotels where service is the whole point. Learn another language properly, maybe Mandarin or Arabic, for the rich guests. Cut every extra cost at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but trying to use it.

S3.say: Hard times, but rich travellers will still want good hotels, maybe more now.
S3.think: A luxury travel boom could help her at a top hotel, but rising rent would leave her and her husband no cushion.
S3.do: Applies to five-star hotels, studies a language for wealthy guests, and cuts household costs.
S3.feel: Anxious, but trying to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a hotel with no people is just a building with beds. Guests will pay for humans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the rich ones will. Robots for cleaning rooms, for the kitchen, for luggage, that's half the hotel staff. The budget hotels would go full robot. I'd be fighting for the few human jobs left in the luxury places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go all in on the luxury side, now, not later. Ask the hotel for any training in guest relations. If we can't save, we'd think about moving somewhere cheaper, even if it's hard on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. The calm on the outside would be hard to keep.

S4.say: A hotel with no people is just a building with beds. Guests will pay for humans.
S4.think: Only rich guests would pay; robots could cover half of hotel staff and budget hotels would go fully robotic.
S4.do: Moves fully into luxury hotels now, seeks guest relations training, and considers moving somewhere cheaper.
S4.feel: Scared, hard to stay calm outside.
